title: Archaeology in a Nutshell
summary: Josh and Chuck explore archaeology as a field, starting with the Indiana Jones image and the discipline's many subfields (forensic, glacial, underwater, Mesopotamian). They cover accidental discoveries (Lascaux cave, Dead Sea Scrolls, a nine-thousand-year-old caribou hunting blind in Lake Huron), the history from Renaissance collecting and Flavio Biondo through Napoleon's Egypt expedition, Richard Colt Hoare, Thomas Jefferson, Charles Lyell's uniformitarianism, and Flinders Petrie's methodology, plus Schliemann at Troy. They explain dating methods, the difference between fieldwork and excavation, grants and permits, geophysical prospecting, meter-by-meter digging, rescue excavations, looting and the black market, ownership and finders-keepers laws by country (New Zealand, Sweden, US, treasure trove), the captain-and-ship salvage tradition, UNESCO 1970 and repatriation, the Nazi Ahnenerbe archaeology expeditions, and a listener mail story about a tip left for a garbage man.

segments.title: Opening banter and Indiana Jones
segments.summary: Hosts open with banter about Indiana Jones and why archaeology is linked to him, noting archaeologists are part explorer, scholar, showman, scientist and historian.

segments.title: Subfields and underwater archaeology
segments.summary: The field is split into many disciplines and subdisciplines, and by geography and period. Underwater archaeology requires careful preservation, and a nine-thousand-year-old caribou hunting blind was found under about 120 feet of water in Lake Huron.

segments.title: Accidental discoveries
segments.summary: Accidental finds are discussed, including the Lascaux cave found by local teens after a storm toppled a tree, and the Dead Sea Scrolls found by a Bedouin shepherd.

segments.title: Renaissance collecting and early antiquarians
segments.summary: Early antiquities were looted and melted for gold. Humanism and the Renaissance gave rise to valuing antiquities for age. Flavio Biondo wrote an early guide to Roman ruins. Royal collecting of Greek and Roman artifacts and the excavation of Pompeii and Herculaneum are covered.

segments.title: Napoleon, Colt Hoare, Jefferson and Lyell
segments.summary: Napoleon formed the Institute of Egypt and published Description of Egypt in 1809. Richard Colt Hoare identified tells in 1812. Thomas Jefferson excavated burial mounds at Monticello. Charles Lyell's uniformitarianism gave a basis for dating through sediment layers.

segments.title: Methodology, Petrie and Schliemann
segments.summary: Flinders Petrie's 1904 book Methods and Aims in Archaeology helped establish responsible excavation. Heinrich Schliemann dug at Troy with less method, while his assistant Wilhelm Dörpfeld took a more methodical approach. The hosts then discuss dating methods including self-dating, relative dating, varve counting, carbon dating, potassium argon dating and thermoluminescence.

segments.title: Archaeology becomes a multidisciplinary science
segments.summary: The field's early focus was dating and cataloging artifacts. In the fifties and sixties archaeologists began asking why changes happened, bringing in experts from other fields and adopting the scientific method.

segments.title: Fieldwork, funding and excavation process
segments.summary: Fieldwork versus excavation is discussed. Research, permits and grants come first, then geophysical prospecting to survey a site, then meter-by-meter digging. Rescue excavations on construction sites, such as Miami and Turkey, are covered.

segments.title: Looting, black market and Peru
segments.summary: Looting continues despite laws and signs. The black market sells artifacts, and dinosaur bones are a hot item. Peru estimates lost artifacts worth about eighteen million dollars and works with the International Council of Museums.

segments.title: Ownership, finders-keepers laws and salvage
segments.summary: Museums long owned much looted material and source countries now seek its return, including Yale and Machu Picchu. Finder laws differ: New Zealand uses a 1976 date, Sweden requires reporting multiple objects, the US uses a hundred-year rule, and treasure trove law applies. Sunken treasure and the captain-stays-with-the-ship tradition are discussed.

segments.title: UNESCO convention and repatriation
segments.summary: The 1970 UNESCO Convention set international standards, though many countries have ratified it and enforcement is weak. Repatriation of artifacts to source countries is discussed, along with the older practice of excavators keeping some finds.

segments.title: Nazi archaeology expeditions
segments.summary: Himmler founded the Ahnenerbe, which ran about eighteen archaeological expeditions to prove German Aryan origins, including Iceland, where a cave was claimed as the Hof. None bore fruit.

segments.title: Learning to spell archaeology and show plugs
segments.summary: Hosts joke about spelling archaeology and the letter-ordering rule, then promote Don't Be Dumb and T-shirts.

segments.title: Listener mail: the tipped garbage man
segments.summary: Emily Crawford writes that her mother left a tip with a card and envelope on an iron horsehead ornament for their small-business garbage man, who likely took the horsehead along with the envelope.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts close by inviting listeners to write in and share stories, and mention the Men at Work film.
